classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied proof stages, selecting SSS then SAS and transferring matching angles and sides between nested triangles. Equal supplementary angles establish perpendicularity; the circle case also requires recognising equal radii.

content.prompt: Each of these problems requires two applications of congruence. The points $O$ and $Z$ are the centres of circles.

spec.description: Kite-shaped DEFG with intersecting diagonals DF and GE; triple ticks on DG and DE and double ticks on GM and ME.
spec.mathematics: DG = DE; GM = ME; D,M,F collinear and G,M,E collinear.
spec.answerVisibility: No equality marks on GF and EF and no right-angle mark.

answer.short: $GD=ED$, $GM=EM$ and $DM$ is common, so $\triangle GDM\equiv\triangle EDM$ (SSS).
answer.worked:
$GD=ED$ and $GM=EM$ (given), and $DM=DM$ (common side).

Therefore $\triangle GDM\equiv\triangle EDM$ (SSS).

answer.short: $\angle DMG=\angle DME$ (matching angles). They sum to $180^\circ$, so both are $90^\circ$ and $DM\perp GE$.
answer.worked:
$\angle DMG=\angle DME$ (matching angles of the congruent triangles in part i).

Since $G,M,E$ are collinear, $\angle DMG+\angle DME=180^\circ$. Thus $\angle DMG=\angle DME=90^\circ$, so $DM\perp GE$.

answer.short: $GM=EM$, $MF$ is common and $\angle GMF=\angle EMF=90^\circ$, so $\triangle GMF\equiv\triangle EMF$ (SAS).
answer.worked:
$GM=EM$ (given) and $MF=MF$ (common side).

Since $D,M,F$ are collinear and $DM\perp GE$, $\angle GMF=\angle EMF=90^\circ$.

Therefore $\triangle GMF\equiv\triangle EMF$ (SAS).

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Hence, show that $GF=EF$. $DEFG$ is called a kite.

answer.worked: From $\triangle GMF\equiv\triangle EMF$, $GF=EF$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).

spec.description: Two intersecting circles with centres O and Z and common points A and B. OA, OB, ZA, ZB, AB and OZ are drawn. A curved annotation leader identifies W at the intersection of AB and OZ.
spec.mathematics: OA = OB and ZA = ZB are radii; A,W,B and O,W,Z are collinear.
spec.answerVisibility: No right-angle or midpoint marks supplied; the W leader is not a locus.

answer.short: $OA=OB$, $ZA=ZB$ (radii) and $OZ$ is common, so $\triangle OAZ\equiv\triangle OBZ$ (SSS).
answer.worked:
$OA=OB$ (radii of the circle centred at $O$), $ZA=ZB$ (radii of the circle centred at $Z$), and $OZ=OZ$ (common side).

Therefore $\triangle OAZ\equiv\triangle OBZ$ (SSS).

answer.short: $\angle AOW=\angle BOW$ (matching angles, since $O,W,Z$ are collinear).
answer.worked:
$\angle AOZ=\angle BOZ$ (matching angles of the congruent triangles in part i).

Since $W$ lies on $OZ$, $\angle AOW=\angle BOW$.

answer.short: $OA=OB$, $OW$ is common and $\angle AOW=\angle BOW$, so $\triangle AOW\equiv\triangle BOW$ (SAS).
answer.worked:
$OA=OB$ (radii), $OW=OW$ (common side), and $\angle AOW=\angle BOW$ (part ii).

Therefore $\triangle AOW\equiv\triangle BOW$ (SAS).

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Hence, show that $OZ$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

answer.short: $AW=BW$ and $\angle OWA=\angle OWB=90^\circ$. Thus $OZ$ bisects $AB$ at right angles.
answer.worked:
$AW=BW$ and $\angle OWA=\angle OWB$ (matching sides and angles of the congruent triangles in part iii).

Since $A,W,B$ are collinear, $\angle OWA+\angle OWB=180^\circ$, so both angles are $90^\circ$.

Thus $OW\perp AB$ and $W$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Since $O,W,Z$ are collinear, $OZ$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
